The arrival of generative artificial intelligence has quietly rewritten the financial grammar of enterprise technology. While traditional software consumption models are based on users, seats or servers, the modern stack is based on tokens, the smallest unit of linguistic and computational work that large language models process. This article looks at AI tokenomics as a formal discipline to manage the cost, value, and scale of intelligence within the organization. It explores the history of the token as the leading measure of information technology, how organizations are developing observability and governance systems to track it and why traditional budgeting methods break down in the recursive requirements of autonomous agents. The three pillars of a mature Tokenomic framework are attributed, predicted and optimized, and the analysis discusses the structural challenges that hinder each of the three steps hidden reasoning tokens, data gravity, and lack of pricing standards among providers. The study also considers the path of hybrid architectures, the emergence of autonomous budget agents, and economic aspects related to the forecasted twenty fourfold increase in the use of tokens by 2030. The findings indicate that those organisations that will see tokens as a strategic currency not a line item will shape the next decade of competitive advantage in digital transformation.

documents.abstract: This study examines the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on students’ stress indicators, particularly perceived stress and its cognitive, behavioral, emotional, and physiological manifestations. The theoretical analysis re-vealed a lack of research addressing this issue, prompting an empirical study involving a sample of 102 stu-dents. The findings indicate that affective engagement with AI contributes to higher levels of perceived stress. At the same time, frequent use of AI reduces perceived stress levels while increasing its cognitive and emo-tional manifestations. Using the technology primarily for educational purposes increases the cognitive and be-havioral manifestations of stress. These results highlight the need to develop psychological programs to pre-vent stress resulting from the adverse effects of AI and to promote its psychologically safe use. They also un-derscore the need for further empirical research to identify other potential consequences of using this technol-ogy.

documents.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has accelerated institutional transformation through data analysis capabilities, process automation, and technology-based decision-making support. However, the increasing use of AI also presents ethical challenges related to transparency, accountability, algorithmic bias, and human responsibility in controlling technology. This study aims to explore how AI-Enabled Prophetic Leadership contributes to building Smart Ethical Governance to support sustainable institutional transformation. This study uses an exploratory qualitative approach involving 24 participants from three institutions that have implemented AI-based digital transformation. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, non-participant observation, and document analysis, then analyzed using thematic analysis techniques. The results of the study show three main findings, namely: (1) the reconstruction of prophetic leadership values (shiddiq, amanah, tabligh, and fathanah) into dimensions of digital integrity, moral accountability, communicative transparency, and ethical intelligence; (2) the integration of prophetic leadership and AI through human-centered decision-making, algorithmic oversight, system transparency, and strengthening organizational competencies; and (3) institutional transformation through structural, cultural, and operational changes. This research produces a conceptual model of the AI-Based Prophetic Ethical Governance Model (APEGM) that positions prophetic leadership as the foundation of values, AI as a decision-support instrument, and human oversight as a technology control mechanism. This research provides theoretical contributions to the development of ethical leadership and AI governance studies and provides practical implications for institutions in building innovative, responsible, and human-value-oriented digital transformations.

documents.abstract: Cognitive sciences have significantly advanced the understanding of human behavior; however, the systematic application of these insights in management remains underdeveloped. This study aims to articulate a comprehensive framework for applying cognitive sciences in management, spanning theoretical foundations to practical tools. Using a Systematic Review approach combined with qualitative content analysis, 40 scholarly sources from databases such as Scopus and Web of Science were analyzed. Findings indicate that Cognitive Management, as an emerging paradigm, organizes the application of cognitive sciences into five key axes: (1) management of cognitive biases (e.g., Devil’s Advocate), (2) choice architecture and nudge (focusing on the design of decision environments), (3) neuro-leadership (using the SCARF model to manage social dynamics), (4) cognitive load management (aimed at optimizing information and process design), and (5) cognitive AI (developing AI systems that interact with and complement human cognition). This framework suggests that, rather than attempting to alter human nature, Cognitive Management leverages the notion of bounded rationality to design environments and organizational processes aligned with the architecture of the mind. While this paradigm provides evidence-based tools that enhance decision-making, leadership, and human resource management, it also faces key challenges related to ethical considerations and the protection of individual autonomy.

This chapter examines the technological interface from a sociotechnical and interdisciplinary perspective.It describes the shift from the functionalist paradigm, which valued products by algorithmic performance, electronic stability and compliance with technical requirements, towards user-centred design, which holds that interactive systems must adapt to people's needs, cognitive limitations and contexts of use.Within this framework, usability and aesthetics are presented not as ornamental or independent attributes but as dimensions to be integrated.The chapter treats hardware and software as a single sociotechnical system: hardware provides the material canvas in which aesthetics first appears, while software shapes the interactive dynamics in which usability is experienced.The graphical user interface (GUI) is therefore addressed as the core of interaction, the space where functional and visual attributes converge.The approach is a conceptual, descriptive-analytical review of human-computer interaction literature, covering event-driven programming and GUI components such as icons, windows, pointing devices, menus and buttons, together with a brief historical account from Xerox PARC to the Macintosh and touchscreen devices.Drawing on this literature, the chapter states that interfaces based on visual metaphors and icons reduce the learning curve and cognitive load, and that an imbalance between hardware and software quickly undermines both aesthetics and actual usability.It concludes that a holistic, interactive approach grounded in user needs is required for products to be competitive, with user-centred design proposed as the framework for integrating usability and aesthetics in organizational settings.

Context: As digital technologies advance rapidly, organizations require analytical frameworks that move beyond subjective intuition and interpret ease of use as a sociotechnical property that regulates business efficiency.Objective: The chapter analyzes the functional dimension of interactive design through the formalization of usability within the corporate environment of organizations.Method: An analytical-conceptual, descriptive and foundational approach was used, based on a systematic review of standards in computer ergonomics and in human-computer interaction (HCI) and on the operationalization of the construct into performance variables and indicators.The chapter examines the definition of usability provided by the ISO 9241-11 standard, its articulation with the ISO 9241-210 standard, Jakob Nielsen's five-attribute model, the conceptual distinction between usability and user experience (UX), and the operational principles of usable design in organizations.Results: According to the analysis, the systematic measurement of effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction optimizes workflows and limits cognitive load, and these dimensions constitute the basis for the quantitative diagnosis of interaction.However, challenges remain, such as the terminological confusion between usability and UX and the difficulty of achieving operational consistency and reversibility.Conclusions: Usability is a necessary, though not sufficient, component of a competitive UX.The formal adoption of the ISO 9241-11 standard is suggested in order to reduce technical support costs, shorten users' learning curves and maximize the perceived value of the product.

Background: Journalism is a high-demand occupation characterised by sustained time pressure, emotional demands, and exposure to potentially distressing events, making occupational burnout and psychological well-being important concerns. This study examined psychological and occupational well-being and burnout-related indicators among journalists in Spain and Germany, focusing on country and gender differences. Methods: This study employed a cross-sectional design. The participants comprised 227 professional journalists (Spain: n = 115; Germany: n = 112; 108 men and 119 women) recruited via non-probability convenience sampling. Workplace well-being, global life satisfaction, happiness, professional quality of life, and burnout were assessed using standardised questionnaires. Descriptive statistics, Pearson’s correlations, and independent-sample t-tests were performed. Welch’s correction was used when required and Holm’s procedure was applied to families with multiple comparisons. Effect sizes were expressed as Cohen’s d with 95% confidence intervals. Results: The mean Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS) total score was 15.61 (standard deviation [SD] = 2.76), while mean scores were 31.22 (SD = 6.30) for compassion satisfaction, 24.75 (SD = 6.20) for Professional Quality of Life (ProQOL) burnout and 20.94 (SD = 13.43) for Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) emotional exhaustion. Workplace resources were positively associated with happiness in the current position (r = 0.57 to 0.74, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). ProQOL burnout and emotional exhaustion were negatively associated with well-being indicators (r = –0.62 to –0.29, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). No statistically significant country differences were identified and the effect sizes were negligible or small. After Holm’s adjustment, women reported higher compassion satisfaction (mean [M] = 33.30, SD = 5.50 vs. M = 28.92, SD = 6.36; d = –0.74), ProQOL burnout (M = 26.59, SD = 5.86 vs. M = 22.67, SD = 6.02; d = –0.66) and emotional exhaustion (M = 24.52, SD = 13.84 vs. M = 16.92, SD = 11.97; d = –0.59). Conclusions: In this non-probability sample, positive occupational and psychological indicators coexisted with burnout-related strain. The results indicate associations rather than causal effects, and highlight the need for further longitudinal and country-adjusted research on journalists’ occupational health.

Multi-agent systems have emerged as a dominant architectural paradigm for applied AI, yet deploying them effectively requires bridging scientific understanding of agent coordination with engineering constraints and real-world application demands. This survey presents a unified perspective on the multi-agent AI landscape, synthesizing research across the science of how multiple LLM-driven agents coordinate, the engineering of systems that implement that coordination under production constraints, and the application-level evidence of where such systems deliver measurable value. We introduce a layered taxonomy of multi-agent capabilities, spanning Agent Primitives, Coordination, Communication, Intelligence, and Assurance. We then organize 13 functionalities into 8 key concepts derived inductively from the literature, situated within the layered taxonomy of multi-agent capabilities: (Agent specialization, Orchestration patterns, Decision making, Context engineering, Learning, Evaluation, Tracing & Monitoring, and Security & Safety). For each concept, we trace its intellectual origins, survey current scientific findings, examine engineering design patterns, and ground the discussion in enterprise deployments. We motivate multi-agent architectures through an analysis of single-agent limitations (including context saturation, instruction-following degradation, tool selection noise, and limited modularity) while acknowledging that multi-agent decomposition is not universally superior and introduces its own coordination overhead. We identify principled criteria for when multi-agent coordination is justified over single-agent designs, and examine the responsible AI mechanisms necessary for trustworthy operation at scale. We conclude by outlining directions for future research on open challenges, including evaluation difficulty, cost efficiency, emergent security threats, and governance in a rapidly shifting regulatory landscape.

Who should represent a human–AI community depends on its institutional strategy, the proposed act, and the relations through which authority and practical competence are constituted. This paper connects representative selection, collective-position formation, external recognition, and continuing cooperation. It distinguishes constituencies, appointing bodies, holders, resource controllers, counterparties, and affected parties. A standard categorical pullback describes the conjunction of internal appointment and counterpart acceptance where required. Constructed constitutional histories and a standard judgment-aggregation countercase show how similar capabilities and consistent constituent judgments can support different arrangements and public positions. Agents can recognize attributed histories and selected norm derivations, acknowledge a documented contribution, and undertake bounded obligations through an authorized procedure. An archive encounter preserves plural origin narratives while enabling a restricted review and an agent’s liaison appointment. A standard proof-path functor describes replay under accepted translations and premises. Historical truth, situated interpretation, normative standing, and an operative undertaking retain distinct grounds. A further case negotiates incompatible public-audit and source-confidentiality requirements through a scoped accommodation. Its continuation examines registry standard changes, authority to hear objections, disconnection, and succession after exit. Recognition and interoperability thus become relations whose governing interfaces can themselves be contested and revised. The analysis also develops commitment stages, resource reservation, revocation, and archival continuity. Primary engagement with representation, configurable governance, recognition theory, electronic institutions, AI delegation, institutional economics, and standards supplies antecedents. Selected empirical studies locate federated governance frictions and asymmetries within their observed settings. The proposed contribution connects collective voice and continuing reception to heterogeneous epistemic means, distributed controllers, and plural institutions. Conditional mathematical results and finite diagnostics retain their assumptions. Observation and later implementation can assess effects on cooperation, human presence, answerability, and opportunities to revise a relation.

documents.abstract: Human–AI communities combine brief contributions with continuing projects, shared resources, and consequential undertakings. This paper develops remedial continuity as a way to investigate whether a live claim can reach an authorized and practically meaningful response through institutional change. A comparative jurisprudential inquiry connects relational powers, plural normative orders, collective identity, resource rights, evidence, and access to remedy. Selected primary legal and philosophical sources retain their jurisdictions, statuses, and argumentative scopes. Developed cases distinguish an operational actor from a represented party, operation-specific responsibility from a whole delegation chain, and claim recognition from the beneficiary and authority of a response. Human interests, protective conduct rules, and possible direct AI claims require their respective grounds. A typed route diagnostic identifies the relevant party, competent forum, lawfully usable evidence, and feasible response. Standard conditional constructions examine transition, archival answerability, jointly feasible schedules, and irreversible response order. A sustained cross-community conflict shows how historical recognition and a successful bounded agreement can coexist with contested permissions, excluded agency questions, external claims, and funding gaps. Further comparisons follow exploitation allegations, translated complaints, shared control, community splits, and continuing duties through changing operational carriers. The framework preserves configurable constitutions and context-sensitive strategies while making the effects of those choices assessable. Its contribution is a specified comparative research architecture and conditional diagnostics; implemented inquiry, independent normative criticism, and jurisdiction-specific analysis are needed to evaluate particular arrangements.

The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into online platforms has created significant trust and safety challenges because AI systems can generate, amplify and distribute digital harms across different platform functions and stages of the AI lifecycle.This study develops a Risk-Adaptive Trust and Safety Governance Framework for AI-Enabled Online Platforms as a methodology for identifying, measuring, prioritising and mitigating digital harm.A systematic literature review and conceptual framework-development design was adopted.Relevant literature published between 2017 and 2024 was examined across major academic databases and authoritative sources, with attention given to AI-enabled digital harms, their determinants, risk assessment, risk classification, platform governance and mitigation strategies.The analysis indicates that AI-enabled digital harm is not limited to technical errors or harmful content but can emerge through data practices, model design, deployment conditions, algorithmic ranking, recommendation, moderation, personalisation and organisational decisions.The study further establishes that effective risk assessment requires multidimensional indicators that consider likelihood, severity, exposure, scale, vulnerability and contextual conditions rather than relying exclusively on technical performance measures.On this basis, the proposed framework connects five interrelated processes: identification of digital harm, examination of its determinants, measurement of risk, classification and prioritisation, and proportionate trust and safety mitigation.The framework adopts a continuous feedback approach in which risk assessment informs intervention and the outcomes of intervention generate evidence for subsequent reassessment.The study concludes that effective AI platform governance requires adaptive, evidence-based and accountable trust and safety mechanisms capable of responding to changing technologies, user behaviour and emerging forms of digital harm.

This paper presents an agentic artificial intelligence framework that detects, diagnoses and resolves hold transactions, which are stuck or failed transactions, in integrated hospital pharmacy environments. Large health systems often run order entry, medication processing, billing, stock and inventory, laboratory, blood bank and automated dispensing software from different vendors, and holds arise at the interfaces where no single vendor sees the whole transaction. Analysts resolve holds manually today, so backlogs build up and stock records drift from physical reality. The research problem is how to automate the repetitive part of this work without weakening audit, inventory accuracy or patient safety. Using a design science approach, the paper develops a taxonomy of five hold causes, a five agent architecture based on a monitor, analyze, plan, execute and knowledge control loop, a tiered autonomy policy with approval gated reprocessing, and an artificial intelligence governance model. A 30 day simulation with 20 replications and a sensitivity analysis evaluate the design. Under stated assumptions, about 82 percent of holds are resolved automatically and mean handling time falls from about 43 to 11 minutes, but the human escalation queue stays bounded only above a break even of about 80 percent automatic resolution. The work indicates that governed agentic automation is a promising option for multivendor hospital pharmacy operations, provided that automatic resolution and false fix rates are confirmed through the staged pilot protocol proposed here.

documents.abstract: Introduction Agentic artificial intelligence systems in education represent a qualitative departure from traditional educational technology. Unlike reactive tools requiring continuous human direction, agentic AI monitors learner states, initiates interventions without requests, and pursues pedagogical objectives independently. Yet this technical sophistication has outpaced theoretical development, leaving fundamental questions unaddressed: How does agent autonomy affect learner agency? When does proactive support enhance versus undermine self-directed learning? What theories adequately address systems demonstrating independent goal pursuit? Methods This study analyzes recent agentic AI research using the ADO-TCM (Antecedents-Decisions-Outcomes-Theories-Contexts-Methods) framework, which traces design logic from problem identification through decisions to outcomes while assessing theoretical grounding, contextual boundaries, and methodological rigor. Following PRISMA guidelines, three researchers independently coded the titles and abstracts of 170 primary studies, achieving substantial agreement. Results As reported in titles and abstracts, the field is characterized by theoretical absence rather than diversity: the vast majority of papers engage no learning theory and invoke AI capabilities as rationale without engaging learning sciences foundations. Alongside this absence, most abstracts do not report whether agents operate autonomously or under supervision, papers addressing multiple problems more often bundle several pedagogical roles in one agent, and most abstracts report outcomes without comparison groups. Because coding was based on titles and abstracts, these gaps describe reported information and require full-text examination before they can be attributed to the underlying research. Discussion Existing theories (e.g., zone of proximal development, cognitive load theory, self-determination theory, activity theory) inadequately address agentic AI's autonomous characteristics. Scaffolding anticipation, autonomy load, and distributed autonomy are offered as conceptual propositions for extending them. We propose theoretical directions, evidence standards, and equity-centered principles to advance agentic AI research from atheoretical demonstration toward theoretically grounded, methodologically rigorous, and equitably distributed practice.

documents.abstract: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) is increasingly envisioned as a transformative force in education, yet research on AGI-driven education remains fragmented across educational stages and rarely incorporates sustainability into system design and evaluation. This systematic review examines how AGI and large language model (LLM)/generative AI technologies reshape education across the learning lifespan and how sustainability can be embedded in AGI-powered education. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and Google Scholar for studies published between 2015 and 2026, using keyword groups related to general intelligence, education, and sustainability. After screening, 85 peer-reviewed studies were included and synthesized through narrative synthesis. Given that full AGI remains unrealized, current LLM and generative AI systems are treated as emergent approximations of AGI’s educational potential. We develop an organizing framework that maps AGI’s transformative roles, key mechanisms, and sustainability implications across early childhood, K–12, higher education, and lifelong learning. The review identifies four emerging application scenarios and introduces a multidimensional sustainability lens encompassing cognitive, economic, social, and ethical–environmental dimensions, extending evaluation beyond conventional academic performance indicators. It also highlights persistent technical, social, and ethical challenges. By integrating stage-specific transformations with a lifespan and sustainability perspective, this review provides a reference and research agenda for the responsible and sustainable integration of AGI into Education 5.0.

This position article offers a conceptual, theory-informed analysis of artificial intelligence (AI) and school leadership. Drawing on Industry 5.0 and international literature, we uniquely examine how leadership for AI is shaped by governance structures, accountability measures and cultural dynamics within centralized education systems. Using the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as a context-specific example, we offer insights into how school leaders, globally, can pursue purposeful and ethical AI integration in reform-intensive systems, concluding with recommendations aligned with human-centered leadership principles.

Supervised land cover mapping of a historical baseline needs reference labels that can no longer be collected in the field. This study documents and evaluates a desk verification workflow that produced Sentinel-2 training samples for a 2019–2020 baseline map of the Lima Puluh coastal landscape, Batu Bara, North Sumatra (about 24,300 ha), where oil palm, paddy, mangrove and aquaculture ponds meet. Candidate points were generated in Google Earth Engine from rule-based frames in two rounds. A multimodal large language model proposed a label and a structured note for each candidate from very-high-resolution basemap chips and Sentinel-2 2019–2020 chips, and the researcher reviewed every proposal. Of 1,114 candidates, 1,024 were reviewed; 450 were confirmed, 364 rejected and 210 left uncertain. A 100 m within-class spacing rule gave 434 training points in seven classes. Frame precision ranged from 0% for index-only water masks to 98% for map-anchored settlement frames. In the priority review of 64 uncertain water and pond points, 58 were excluded, mainly because of mixed land–water pixels, ambiguous fallow plots and water that appeared after 2019; the researcher overrode 1 of 64 proposals. Targeted additions of oil palm and coastal paddy points raised spatially cross-validated kappa from 0.823 to 0.860 and, on a blind validation sample of 300 points, overall accuracy from 0.850 to 0.873 and paddy producer’s accuracy from 0.709 to 0.846. AI-assisted desk verification can supply auditable training data when field access is impossible, provided that a human decides every label and accuracy is estimated independently.

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare systems is transforming not only clinical practice but also the educational pathways preparing future healthcare professionals. This pilot study examines the pedagogical use of AI-assisted conversational simulation in healthcare professions education, comparing AI-based virtual patient interaction with traditional role-play. A randomized parallel-group pilot study with a post-test-only design involved 56 students enrolled in the Master's Degree Program in Diagnostic Technical Healthcare Professions at the University of Foggia. Participants were randomly assigned, through stratified randomization with permuted blocks, to AI-assisted communication training (Group A, n = 28) or traditional role-play with human facilitators (Group B, n = 28) in 1:1 allocation. The 20-hour educational intervention integrated Medical Humanities, healthcare communication, experiential learning, and simulation-based education; Group A trained with a publicly available custom GPT virtual patient using the voice mode of ChatGPT Plus. Communication self-efficacy (SE-12), the primary outcome, was significantly higher in Group A (mean difference 5.74, 95% CI 3.08–8.40; Cohen's d = 1.18, 95% CI 0.60–1.76), an effect that persisted after adjusting for prior AI experience. Communication apprehension (PRCA-24), the secondary outcome, did not differ significantly between groups, either overall or on any of the four subscales. These preliminary findings suggest that AI-assisted conversational simulation may usefully complement traditional communication training and contribute to the broader debate on digital literacy in health professions curricula. The post-test-only design, the single assessment at 7 days, and the use of a non-validated Italian translation of the SE-12 limit inference about causality and durability.

documents.abstract: A challenge for organizations is that AI-driven digital transformation introduces both unseen and unprecedented risk. From a systems perspective, such risk develops between formal constraints and situated practice; organizational members must interpret AI outputs in context and determine whether to accept, modify, or override them. Risk becomes more apparent when outputs are unexpected, system behavior is difficult to explain, or experience with existing tools raises concerns. Such interactions among organizational members and AI systems serve as a form of distributed sensing, whereby indications of risk are detected and interpreted jointly and iteratively rather than through centralized monitoring. The growing prevalence of generative and agentic AI makes this capacity relevant to organizations, as members initiate actions with AI systems under conditions that cannot be fully specified in advance. AI-driven digital transformation therefore calls for organizations to maintain ongoing interpretation and adjustment, enabling them to balance control with coordinated, adaptive action while remaining responsive to emergent risks.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is being integrated across various fields. AI advancements have catalyzed a paradigm shift in psychological assessment and intervention, aiming to rapidly transform how mental health and psychological imbalance are assessed, monitored, and treated. In this research, we examine the role of AI in the early detection of affective and cognitive disorders, with a focus on depression, anxiety, and stress-related psychopathologies using emotion recognition technologies and predictive modeling. We explore how affective computing techniques such as facial expression analysis, speech recognition, and natural language processing are integrated within digital mental health platforms for efficient therapeutic alliance, accurate clinical decision-making, and boosted user engagement. In addition, this research investigates the effects of human-computer interaction in an AI-powered mental health context, addressing constructs such as user trust, engagement, and cognitive reliance on autonomous systems. A critical analysis of ethical and governance factors demonstrated several pitfalls that hinder AI-driven mental health adoption. These include algorithm opacity and bias, non-compliance with regulatory frameworks and data protection policies, and inequitable access to existing platforms. The interdisciplinary synthesis employed in this study provides evidence-based insight with strategic recommendations for developing, deploying, and regulating AI-driven mental health solutions in healthcare systems.

documents.abstract: Selecting health insurance involves comparing different plans according to various parameterssuch as premiums, coverages, waiting periods, exclusions, co-payment and others which areunique to each provider. Artificial intelligence has been applied to various aspects of the insurancevalue chain, yet the relevant literature can be found scattered in recommendation, cost prediction,risk assessment, customer analytics, conversational advice, explainability and fraud detection. Thispaper provides a structured survey of 24 research papers included in the synopsis of thisdissertation with regard to their research questions, methodology, results and limitations. Thisreview will distinguish between direct plan recommendation and its adjacent predictive tasks andcompare the reviewed research studies in terms of their research questions, methodologies, resultsand limitations. It becomes clear from the literature review that there is at least some directevidence of utility-based or feedback-based recommendations for health insurance plans, whereasthere are many machine learning and deep learning studies that deal with cost, claim, fraud or crossselling but not with plan selection. Some conversational interface studies appear to emergealthough there is little evidence about the quality of recommendation and user-centeredexplanations.

Chemical risk assessment is undergoing a fundamental transition driven by the need for human-relevant, mechanistically informed, and animal-free approaches. Digital infrastructures that integrate New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), including computational models and emerging artificial intelligence (AI) tools, are increasingly considered drivers of this transition. However, their regulatory uptake depends on several factors, including trust, transparency, scientific validity, and the sustainability of the infrastructures. This paper summarises the outcomes from a multi-stakeholder expert workshop, jointly organised by the European Centre for Ecotoxicology and Toxicology of Chemicals (ECETOC), the VHP4Safety project, and the ONTOX project, focusing on the application of AI-supported digital infrastructures in human health risk assessment of chemicals. The workshop explored technical, regulatory, and governance challenges associated with the integration of AI-supported NAMs into regulatory workflows. This was achieved through demonstrations of two recently developed platforms, the Virtual Human Platform (VHP) and Ontology-driven Probabilistic Risk Assessment (OPRA). Key insights highlight that transparency, traceability and explainability tailored to user needs are necessary for adoption and regulatory acceptance, as well as sustained engagement with regulators. Participants emphasised the importance of platform interoperability, and the need for targeted training for end users. Furthermore, long-term sustainability of digital infrastructures emerged as a critical concern, requiring distinct governance beyond project-based funding. Based on these insights, actionable recommendations for the design, implementation, and governance of AI-supported digital infrastructures to enable regulatory uptake of NAMs are reported. These recommendations are intended to inform developers, regulators and stakeholders advancing next-generation chemical risk assessment across regulatory domains.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are widespread across fields such as healthcare, finance, employment, and criminal justice, with a substantial impact on the lives of individuals and society. However, it has been established that AI systems perpetuate existing social inequalities, particularly through biases that are not easily discernible. Such biases are embedded in the technical and social structures of artificial intelligence systems, making them difficult to detect. These biases challenge the concept of Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI), which recognizes diversity as the acknowledgment of individual differences, equity as fairness and equal access, and inclusion as the value placed on all participants. This study argues that fairness in artificial intelligence systems cannot be achieved by focusing solely on their technical aspects, necessitating a holistic approach. This study employs a two-phase mixed-methods design. Phase 1 applies computational content analysis to 360 occupational narratives generated by ChatGPT across four countries (Canada, Germany, India, and Bangladesh) using gender-neutral prompts to examine whether professions are predominantly associated with one gender and whether these patterns remain consistent across regions. Phase 2 examines the extent to which students recognize potential bias in AI, their trust in AI for consequential decision-making, and how these perceptions relate to themes in EDI and AI ethics scholarship. By combining output-level bias analysis with user perception data, this study identifies the empirical foundations necessary for future EDI-AI co-design frameworks, outlining the sociotechnical dimensions that such frameworks must address to be effective.

documents.abstract: AI systems are widely used in recruitment screening, job allocation, performance evaluation, remuneration decisions, promotion and dismissal. Compared with traditional human management, algorithmic management can improve information-processing efficiency and assist employers in making complex workplace decisions. This article employs doctrinal legal analysis to examine the regulation of AI-driven employment decisions under the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), anti-discrimination law and the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth). Drawing on Mobley v Workday Inc and Houston Federation of Teachers v Houston Independent School District, it identifies the practical limitations of the existing legal framework. The analysis finds that Australian law provides partial protection, but remains fragmented and reactive. Workers generally obtain remedies only after an adverse decision has occurred, while the current framework lacks adequate pre-deployment disclosure, risk assessment, independent auditing and meaningful human review. It recommends prior disclosure, individualised reasons for adverse decisions, restrictions on solely automated decisions, clear employer accountability, algorithmic impact assessments, periodic independent audits and worker participation. These reforms would not prohibit workplace AI; rather, they would establish a more appropriate balance between technological efficiency, fairness, accountability and worker protection.

documents.abstract: Natural hazards are not purely physical phenomena but coupled human–environment systems in which consequences are shaped by behavioral, infrastructural, and institutional dynamics interacting with physical processes. While current Geographic Information System (GIS)-based digital twins, enhanced by artificial intelligence (AI), have advanced our capacity to monitor and predict physical hazard dynamics, they leave the social and behavioral dimensions of disaster largely unrepresented. This gap in situational intelligence constitutes a critical failure in smart disaster management, such as evacuation gridlock, warning non-compliance, and cascading infrastructure failures triggered by human decisions. This chapter discusses Cognitive Spatial Intelligence Systems (CSIS) as a new framework that addresses this gap by integrating five intelligence layers: Spatial Intelligence (GIS), System Intelligence (digital twins), Predictive Intelligence (AI and machine learning), Social Behavioral Intelligence (agent-based modeling, ABM), and Decision Intelligence (Environmental Decision Support Tools, EDST). Each layer answers a distinct scientific question that the others cannot resolve: where, what is happening, what will happen, how will people and systems respond, and what should we do. The chapter traces the evolution of spatial intelligence from static cartography through digital twins to CSIS; argues for ABM as the behavioral simulation engine for coupled human–environment hazard systems; and grounds the framework in the California wildfire system as a case study. This framework lets emergency managers anticipate behavioral responses, including evacuation decisions, traffic bottlenecks, warning compliance, and physical hazard forecasts. Integrating social simulation into operational digital twins will shift disaster management from reactive response toward active, behavior-aware decision support.

In the medical field, healthcare professionals often need to diagnose and treat patients based on their descriptions and disease characteristics. During this process, ChatGPT can serve as an auxiliary tool, offering professional advice and supporting clinical decisions. After treating patients, healthcare professionals typically need to provide follow-up health education, such as explaining diagnoses, prescriptions, treatment plans, and necessary precautions. ChatGPT can handle these tasks on their behalf. Utilizing the UTAUT2 model framework, this study incorporates additional variables such as trust, privacy risks, salary, and education level to understand the factors influencing healthcare professionals' willingness to use ChatGPT for job assistance. Surveys were conducted among healthcare professionals serving in medical institutions at the regional level and above, and data was analyzed using descriptive statistics and structural equation modeling. The study results can serve as a reference for healthcare institutions planning to implement relevant information technologies.

documents.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and journalistic practice in Nigeria, focusing on professional competence, ethical challenges and journalists’ perceptions of news credibility. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among practising journalists across print, broadcast and digital media organisations. Data from 392 respondents were analysed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha reliability analysis, Pearson’s product-moment correlation and multiple regression. AI applications were most commonly used for grammar checking and editing (77.0%), content generation (73.0%) and automated transcription (69.1%). Respondents reported moderate-to-high perceived professional competence (M = 3.48), alongside comparatively lower scores for identifying inaccuracies and independently verifying AI-generated information. Ethical challenges were rated highly (M = 4.04), particularly inadequate organisational guidelines, misinformation risks and excessive dependence on AI. Journalists’ perceived news credibility score was also high (M = 4.08), reflecting strong support for human editorial supervision, independent fact-checking and transparency. The regression model showed professional competence as a positive predictor and ethical challenges as a negative predictor of journalists’ perceived news credibility. The study concludes that responsible AI integration requires continuous professional training, institutional ethical guidelines and strengthened editorial oversight.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can support business managers by forecasting demand, identifying operational exceptions, andsummarizing information. Its contribution depends on how firms incorporate these outputs into decisions and assess theconsequences. This article develops a framework for AI-assisted decision-making through a conceptual synthesis of selected research on organizational decision structures, AI capabilities, and workplace productivity. The framework comprises four stages: defining the business decision and its baseline, assigning decision authority, piloting AI in the workflow, and evaluating business outcomes before expanding its use. An illustrative inventory replenishment case demonstrates how forecast accuracy, managerial overrides, and service levels can be assessed together. The case shows why an improvement in forecast accuracy can leave ordering decisions unchanged and why lower stockout rates should be evaluated alongside inventory costs. The article’s contribution is to connect AI implementation to decision accountability and measurable operational outcomes. The framework requires empirical validation across business functions and organizational settings.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing information technology (IT) project management with intelligent automation, predictive analytics, and data-driven project decisions over project lifecycles. Nevertheless, even though AI may enhance operational efficiency, the implementation of this technology has witnessed technological, organizational, and ethical issues, which can cripple the impact of a project. This paper has critically analyzed the advantages and limitations of the use of AI in IT project management with a particular interest in the implications of AI for technical project managers and performance in organizations. An ordered literature review and thematic synthesis of the related publications on IEEE Xplore are suggested to analyze the existing evidence on AI-based scheduling, resource allocation, risk prediction, and project governance. Special consideration is made for relationships such as technological capabilities, organizational readiness, data quality, and human oversight. The article further addresses the issue of whether the enhancement of operational efficiency will inevitably lead to the sustainability of project success, in particular, when the complexity of integration, bias in algorithms, the problem of cybersecurity, and labour constraints are not well managed. The research seeks to bridge these dimensions in order to come up with an evidence-based framework, which would direct responsible AI adoption within the management of IT projects. It is expected to provide a better understanding of the conditions in which AI may be used to assist in the delivery of a project, without jeopardizing managerial responsibility, transparency, and organizational control.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities for learning in higher education while raising concerns about academic integrity, privacy, bias, and misinformation. This study examined AI literacy and ethical AI utilization among second-year Bachelor of Secondary Education major in Science students at City College of Calapan and investigated their relationship as a basis for proposing an institutional framework. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was employed, involving 43 respondents purposively selected from a population of 48 students. Data were analyzed using weighted means and Pearson’s correlation coefficient. Findings revealed high AI literacy in technical knowledge (M = 2.77) and prompting (M = 2.58), but low literacy in critical evaluation (M = 2.42). Ethical utilization was rated low across academic integrity compliance (M = 1.82), ethical awareness and data privacy (M = 2.17), and bias and misinformation mitigation (M = 2.43). The overall relationship between AI literacy and ethical utilization was not statistically significant (r = −0.135, p = 0.389). However, technical knowledge demonstrated a significant moderate negative relationship with bias and misinformation mitigation (r = −0.458, p = 0.002). These findings suggest that technical competence alone does not necessarily translate into responsible AI use. Accordingly, an Institutional Artificial Intelligence Program and Policy Framework adapted from Bilgin’s responsible AI framework was proposed. It comprises AI literacy development, AI utilization policy, AI detection and support tools, monitoring and support, and ethical awareness. The framework emphasizes responsible, ethical, and competent AI utilization through institutional guidance, critical evaluation, academic accountability, and continuing development initiatives for students and faculty.

documents.abstract: This article theorises an emergent training economy in which selected forms of human cognitive, evaluative, corrective, annotative and creative activity become inputs into the training, alignment, evaluation, validation or optimisation of generative AI systems. It develops AI training labour as the analytical category naming these contributions across contracted, precarious and unrecognised arrangements, with particular attention to weakly compensated or institutionally obscured activity. Drawing on digital labour theory, platform political economy and critical data studies, the article argues that generative AI reconfigures platform capitalism by creating a productive route through which selected digital participation can contribute to model development alongside advertising, subscription, cloud and rent-based accumulation. It distinguishes three evidentiary statuses: documented, where technical incorporation is publicly established; inferred, where a credible incorporation pathway exists but actual use is not independently confirmed; and governance risk, where disclosure is insufficient to determine whether incorporation occurs. These are analytically separate from labour status, which ranges from contracted and paid to unpaid and unrecognised. The argument is probed across routine interface interaction, creative production and educational deployment. The training economy proposition specifies the conditions under which human interaction becomes an appropriable input into AI productive capacity, and identifies supporting and disconfirming evidence. Advanced as a tendency rather than a settled regime, the framework connects micro-level labour relations to value extraction, infrastructural concentration and governance in AI-driven digital economies.

documents.abstract: This study examined public school teachers’ artificial intelligence (AI) utilization competence, access to AI resources, and attitudes toward AI use in instructional planning in the Baliwasan District, Zamboanga City, during School Year 2026–2027. Using a quantitative descriptive-comparative and correlational design, the study surveyed 83 teachers from selected elementary, junior high, and senior high schools, identified through purposive sampling, who participated voluntarily. Data were collected through Google Forms using a researcher-developed questionnaire subjected to expert validation and pilot testing among 30 teachers excluded from the main sample. Analyses included the arithmetic mean, one-way analysis of variance, and the r-value. Teachers reported high AI utilization competence and access, alongside positive to very positive attitudes, although connectivity during working hours and institution-supported resources emerged as relative constraints. No statistically significant differences were detected by teaching level. Conventional ANOVA identified differences across years-in-service groups for all three outcomes and across educational-attainment groups for competence and attitudes, but not access; these remained provisional because of small, unequal subgroups and variance violations. AI utilization competence and AI access were strongly and positively associated with attitudes, although these associations do not establish causation. The study concludes that teachers’ attitudes toward AI in instructional planning are closely linked to their competence and access. It recommends needs-based professional learning, dependable technological resources, and practical guidance on responsible AI use. As evidence from a nonprobability sample, the results inform context-specific planning rather than population-wide conclusions.

This study examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Green Recruitment Practices and its impact on employee engagement and retention. Integrating AI with Green Human Resource Management enables organizations to digitize recruitment, reduce paper consumption, minimize unnecessary travel, improve candidate screening and matching, and communicate sustainability-oriented employment values. AI can support candidate sourcing, resume screening, virtual assessments, interview scheduling, candidate communication and recruitment analytics. However, organizations must also address concerns relating to fairness, transparency, privacy, algorithmic bias and excessive automation. Following the structure of the supplied model paper, the present study adopts a quantitative approach using a structured questionnaire and an illustrative sample of 300 respondents. Frequency analysis, Chi-square, ANOVA, correlation, and multiple regression are used to examine the relationships among AI-enabled green recruitment practices, employee engagement, and retention. The illustrative findings indicate significant associations between AI-enabled green recruitment and employee engagement and retention intention. Fairness and transparency, perceived environmental responsibility and employee engagement also emerge as important factors associated with retention. The study recommends human oversight, transparent AI governance, monitoring of algorithmic bias, responsible data management, digital, paperless recruitment, and alignment between recruitment promises and actual green organizational practices. The study concludes that AI can strengthen Green Recruitment Practices and contribute to employee engagement and retention when technological efficiency is combined with authentic sustainability and responsible HR management.

Artificial intelligence (AI) plays an increasingly central role in organizations’ digital transformation. There is growing scholarly interest in how AI supports innovation, that is, how activities and processes aimed at producing novel ideas, problem solutions or other outputs can be enabled by …

Suggestion systems play an important role in encouraging employee participation, improving organizational processes, fostering innovation, and enhancing productivity. However, traditional suggestion systems often face challenges such as the accumulation of unevaluated ideas, repetitive submissions, lengthy evaluation procedures, and a lack of transparent and integrated assessment mechanisms.This presentation explores how artificial intelligence can transform organizational suggestion systems, covering the entire process from idea registration and enrichment to preliminary screening, analysis, and evaluation. It first introduces AI-powered assistants that can convert raw notes and initial ideas into structured proposals, enrich technical and economic information through interactive questioning, identify similar or duplicate submissions, and connect new ideas to the organization's existing knowledge and previous experiences.The presentation then examines the intelligent idea evaluation cycle, including preliminary screening, multi-criteria scoring, impact simulation, and hybrid decision-making. Particular attention is given to AI agents designed to identify similar proposals, analyze supporting documents and evidence, assign preliminary scores based on approved criteria and weights, identify strengths and weaknesses, and flag proposals requiring further technical, financial, or legal assessment by experts.In the practical section, an AI-powered Idea Evaluation Agent is introduced, and its application is demonstrated through the analysis of a sample organizational proposal. The presentation also highlights essential requirements for successful implementation, including data confidentiality, algorithmic transparency, integration with organizational knowledge management systems, and maintaining human oversight in final decision-making.The main objective is to demonstrate how artificial intelligence can transform traditional, administrative suggestion systems into intelligent, transparent, and effective mechanisms that convert employees' ideas into organizational value and innovation.

documents.abstract: Clinician educators occupy a demanding role at the intersection of clinical practice, teaching, and scholarship. Given their teaching roles, they are expected to contribute in particular to health professions education scholarship, yet many have little protected time. AI tools have emerged as practical support for 2 of the time-intensive aspects of scholarly activities: conducting early-stage literature reviews and improving scholarly writing. The rapidly expanding AI landscape has made it increasingly difficult to distinguish purpose-built scholarly platforms from general-purpose AI assistants. As a result, many clinician educators remain uncertain about which tools are appropriate for academic work and how they can be used responsibly. Additionally, the barriers are often as much institutional as individual. Limited protected time, access to experienced mentors, methodological expertise, editorial support, and library services all shape the ability of clinician educators to engage in scholarship. Although AI tools may reduce some of the burdens associated with literature review and writing, they should not be viewed as substitutes for these institutional supports. This viewpoint is intended for clinician educators seeking practical guidance on integrating AI into health professions education scholarship. Our aim is not to provide a systematic review, an exhaustive list of platforms, or an endorsement or ranking of any platform, but rather to offer a practical overview of selected AI tools that we have found useful for health professions education research. These tools include Consensus, Elicit, Scite, Litmaps, ResearchRabbit, Paperpal, Jenni AI, Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot. We group these tools into 6 functional categories and discuss their strengths and limitations across different stages of the scholarly workflow, drawing on vendor documentation and our own experience rather than formal comparative testing, while emphasizing the importance of selecting tools that align with specific scholarly tasks. Since overreliance on AI risks diminishing creative scholarly competencies, we distinguish productive cognitive support, in which AI reduces routine workload, from epistemic off-loading, in which interpretation and judgment are delegated to AI, and argue for using AI as a scaffold that enhances, rather than replaces, intellectual engagement. We also address some ethical considerations, including hallucinated content, citation inaccuracies, transparency in disclosure, and subscription costs. Ultimately, responsible integration of AI into scholarship will require not only appropriate tool selection but also the continued cultivation of the critical thinking and scientific reasoning that define academic scholarship.

documents.abstract: Background: Large language models are increasingly used to assist scholarly peer review, but there is limited evidence about how authors judge their feedback and use it to revise their papers. Methods: We studied authors' experiences of receiving an auxiliary AI review alongside human reviews in three computer-science cohorts: LifeCLEF 2025, LifeCLEF 2026, and CVWW 2026. Post-review questionnaires yielded 92 responses concerning 71 papers. We summarized closed-ended answers using descriptive statistics and examined free-text responses through thematic analysis. Results: Most responses rated the AI review useful (82/92 (89%), and 82/92 (89%) reported using at least some of its suggestions in revision. Authors reported that AI identified issues missed by human reviewers ((76/92 (83%). However, 44/92 (48%) trusted AI feedback less than human feedback, and 58/92 (63%) reported incorrect or misleading comments. Authors valued suggestions that improved clarity and reproducibility, but also described overlooked evidence, inappropriate demands, and difficulty finding useful comments within lengthy reviews. They emphasized the need to check AI feedback and retain control over how their manuscripts were processed. Future review by both humans and AI was supported by 85/92 (92%); 83/92 (90%) preferred advance notice and 73/92 (79%) supported explicit consent. Conclusions: Authors often found AI reviews useful for revision without trusting them as much as human reviews. These exploratory findings favor a supplementary role for AI, with human oversight, clear disclosure, and author consent. They do not establish that AI can replace human reviewers or improve manuscript quality.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT are rapidly entering language teacher education, yet little is known about how pre-service teachers negotiate these tools during authentic instructional planning over time. Drawing on distributed cognition and a mini-c/little-c account of pedagogical creativity, this qualitative study examined how pre-service English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers perceived and negotiated ChatGPT's role in lesson design, critical evaluation, and collaborative reflection across one semester. Twenty-four senior pre-service teachers at a Turkish state university, all completing a school practicum, submitted weekly reflective narratives (n = 232) and took part in end-of-semester semi-structured interviews (n = 24). The data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Six themes were constructed: pedagogical affordances; perceived pedagogical and cognitive risks; human-AI co-creation; epistemic evaluation and validation routines; collaborative reflection and peer scaffolding; and recommendations for teacher education. Participants did not describe ChatGPT as a source of creativity in itself; rather, they located pedagogical creativity in their own iterative constraining, rejecting, and localizing of AI output. At the same time, they reported that offloading pedagogical reasoning, as opposed to routine production, weakened both their planning and its classroom enactment. Verification of AI output was frequently collective, taking place in peer and mentor debriefings. The study offers an account of how novice teachers described negotiating the division of cognitive labor with GenAI and derives three data-grounded implications for language teacher education: assessing design processes rather than products alone, auditing AI output for accuracy and bias, and teaching iterative co-design.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become pervasive in students’ academic activities, yet the mechanisms linking acceptance, ethical concern, and actual use remain underexplored in non-Western higher education contexts. This study extends the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) by incorporating AI-related ethical concern as an additional predictor and tests the resulting model on GenAI use among Indonesian university students. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 560 students who had prior GenAI experience, and the data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The findings show that students mainly used GenAI for initial information searches, literature-source searches, concept clarification, and academic document analysis. Perceived behavioral control was the strongest predictor of behavioral intention, followed by attitude. Subjective norms were not significant, whereas AI-related ethical concern had a small but significant negative effect. Behavioral intention was positively associated with self-reported actual GenAI use. The model explained 45.7% of the variance in behavioral intention and 23.9% of actual behavior. Overall, the findings suggest that perceived behavioral control and attitude are the primary correlates of GenAI-use intention, whereas AI-related ethical concern provides only a small additional restraint signal. The results emphasize the importance of AI literacy, clear task-level guidance, and ethical self-efficacy in higher education while warranting cautious interpretation given the cross-sectional and self-reported nature of the data.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding access to occupational information, educational pathways and personalized exploration in career guidance. However, AI-generated recommendations do not necessarily lead to informed, autonomous or responsible career decisions, particularly among secondary-school students whose interests, identities and decision-making competencies are still developing. This paper proposed the AI–Critical Thinking–Human Guidance (AI–CT–HG) framework, an original conceptual model for integrating AI-supported exploration, critical thinking and human guidance in secondary school career development. The framework comprises five interconnected stages: self-awareness, AI-supported exploration, critical evaluation, reflective human dialogue, and informed decision-making followed by action and review. It was developed through a conceptual synthesis of literature on career construction, planned happenstance, critical thinking, AI in education and human-centred AI governance. The model positions AI as an exploratory resource rather than an authority that determines career choices. Critical thinking serves as the mechanism for evaluating generated information, identifying uncertainty and comparing alternatives, while human guidance provides contextual interpretation, ethical oversight and support for student agency. Transparency, privacy, fairness, accessibility and accountability operate as cross-cutting principles. Practical implications include a structured school-based learning sequence and proposed indicators for assessing the quality of students’ career reasoning. Because the framework has not yet been empirically tested, the paper provides a conceptual foundation for pilot studies and evaluation in diverse educational settings.

documents.abstract: Type of the article: Research ArticleMajed Salem Alsuhaimi - Corresponding author, email: suhaimims@kfsc.edu.saAbstractArtificial intelligence deployment in banking compliance represents one of the most significant workplace transformations in financial services, yet scholarly understanding of how middle managers navigate this transformation remains limited. This qualitative study examines how 18 middle managers across three Saudi banks experienced and adapted to AI-driven role change. Using theory-informed abductive analysis grounded in organizational role theory, the research identifies structural role ambiguity – existential uncertainty about whether roles persist in recognizable form following technological implementation – as theoretically distinctive from traditional role ambiguity.Key findings demonstrate that 89% of participants experienced structural role ambiguity, 83% engaged in active multi-stakeholder role negotiation across organizational hierarchies, 78% employed strategic framing to position AI as augmentation rather than replacement, and all 18 experienced compressed implementation timelines (4-6 months). Compressed implementation velocity functioned as a contextual condition: rapid deployment intensified initial ambiguity through overwhelming organizational simultaneity while paradoxically accelerating resolution through forcing mechanisms.Theoretically, the study makes four contributions to organizational role theory: identifying structural role ambiguity as theoretically distinctive; demonstrating multi-stakeholder rather than dyadic role negotiation; showing that managers exercise significant agency through strategic framing; and clarifying how implementation shapes role transformation temporal dynamics. Empirically, the study provides an in-depth qualitative examination of AI’s impact on compliance professionals in compressed implementation contexts. Practically, the work identifies actionable competencies and strategic guidance for organizational stakeholders.

Generative artificial intelligence can support programming learning, but complete solutions may reduce opportunities to practice critical thinking. This study examined a pedagogical agent guided by the Trigger-Process-Respond framework, which organized questioning, comparison, evidence requests, and reflection across debugging, code review, and post-task reflection. In a six-week quasi-experiment, 60 first-year computer science students in two intact classes at a Chinese university completed three sequential programming tasks. One class used the agent, and the other received conventional instructor feedback. Critical thinking was assessed with the Chinese version of the California Critical Thinking Skills Test, and dialogue records documented students’ reasoning responses. In these two classes, the agent-supported class had higher posttest scores after adjustment for pretest scores. Within the fixed feedback sequences, questioning was followed by more analytical responses, comparison by more evaluative responses, and evidence requests by more argumentative responses. Exploratory analyses linked reflection feedback with reasoning in the next task, particularly between the first two tasks. These findings suggest that stage-structured generative AI feedback can engage students in reasoning during supported programming dialogue.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming increasingly common in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education, but its role in students’ critical thinking (CT) remains unclear. This systematic literature review examines how students interact with GenAI, the factors influencing these interactions, and their relationships with CT-related processes in STEM learning. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore and identified 204 records, of which 17 empirical studies met the inclusion criteria. Six clusters of CT-related processes were found through narrative and thematic synthesis: strategic questioning and task framing; interpretation and analytical decomposition; comparison, evaluation, and verification; error detection and corrective modification; justification, judgment, and independent decision-making; and reflection, metacognition, and self-regulation. Across the included studies, interactions involving questioning AI-generated solutions, verifying their accuracy, examining alternatives, and revising initial interpretations were associated with CT-related processes. Conversely, reliance on GenAI to perform essential reasoning tasks or uncritical acceptance of AI-generated responses may limit opportunities for independent reasoning. These findings suggest that the nature of student–GenAI interactions, particularly the extent to which students retain cognitive responsibility, is important for understanding how GenAI relates to CT processes. Based on the synthesis, we propose an evidence-informed conceptual framework that links student–GenAI interactions, cognitive responsibility, and CT-related processes with personal, instructional, and task-related factors. The framework is derived from the reviewed evidence and requires further empirical validation. However, methodological heterogeneity and limited direct measurement of independent CT outcomes prevent definitive conclusions about whether GenAI improves students’ critical-thinking ability. The review highlights the importance of designing STEM learning activities that encourage questioning, verification, reflection, and independent judgment when interacting with GenAI. Further experimental and longitudinal research is needed to validate the proposed framework and examine how student–GenAI interactions influence critical-thinking development over time.

documents.abstract: Rich economies pay well, yet most of their employees are not engaged. Gallup’s 2026 global survey puts engagement at 20% worldwide and at 12% in Europe, against 31% in the United States and Canada. This paper asks what, besides pay, sustains motivation where pay is already high. It combines secondary analysis of public data with a structured synthesis of meta-analyses and large surveys. Across 18 high-income countries whose income per head differs by a factor of 3.4, national income was unrelated to engagement (Spearman ρ = 0.22, permutation p = .37; 0.8 percentage points per doubling of income, 95% CI − 6.8 to 8.5), and among 14 European countries the correlation was − 0.03. Regions dominated by high-income economies score far higher on life evaluation (52% thriving against 31%) but not on engagement (21% against 22%). Pay level correlates only .15 with job satisfaction, explaining about 2% of its variance, whereas motivational and social work characteristics explain 34% and a further 17%. Pay is nonetheless not trivial: 63% of Americans who quit in 2021 cited low pay (95% CI 60% to 66%), as often as lack of advancement and more often than feeling disrespected (57%). Intrinsic motivation predicts performance (ρ = .21 to .45, k = 183), while financial incentives add most for the quantity of output, and a four-day week at unchanged pay reduced burnout from 2.83 to 2.38 on a five-point scale. Pay works as a threshold and a signal of fairness. Beyond it, motivation is sustained by work design, meaning, respect, development and control of time. The evidence is cross-sectional and uneven in quality, and the paper says where it is thin.

Multigrade teachers face unique instructional challenges as they simultaneously manage learners from different grade levels, particularly in rural school settings where access to educational resources and technology is often limited. Although artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been recognized as a potential tool for enhancing teaching and learning, limited research has explored how multigrade teachers in rural Philippine classrooms perceive, utilize, and navigate the integration of AI into their instructional practices. Addressing this gap, this study explored the perceptions, practices, perceived benefits, challenges, and support needs of multigrade teachers in integrating AI into their teaching. A qualitative case study approach was employed, involving ten (10) multigrade teachers from Kadingilan II District, Division of Bukidnon, during School Year 2026–2027. Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and classroom observations. The findings revealed that teachers perceived AI as a supportive instructional assistant rather than a replacement for their professional roles. Based on their experiences, AI helped facilitate lesson preparation, differentiated instruction, and assessment. However, they emphasized that teacher judgment, creativity, and personal interaction with learners remain essential. The major challenges identified included limited internet connectivity, inaccuracies in AI-generated materials, cultural mismatches, and the risk of over-reliance on AI. To address these concerns, teachers practiced critical evaluation of AI-generated outputs, contextual adaptation of instructional materials, and peer collaboration. Furthermore, teachers identified practical, classroom-focused training, reliable internet connectivity, adequate technological devices, offline AI resources, and clear guidelines on ethical use, data privacy, and academic integrity as essential support mechanisms. The study concludes that AI has potential as a supplementary teaching tool in multigrade classrooms, particularly when supported by adequate resources, professional development, and responsible use. The reported benefits reflect teachers' experiences and perceptions rather than measured improvements in instructional effectiveness. These findings highlight the importance of context-responsive support in promoting meaningful and equitable AI integration in rural multigrade education.

As artificial intelligence systems move from informing decisions to taking actions, the central governance question shifts from what a system can do to what it may do. This paper argues that capability and authority are distinct and that institutions lose control when they treat one as the other. Capability is the power to do something and is possessed by the actor. Authority is the legitimate right to decide and act; it is granted, bounded, accountable and revocable. A system cannot create legitimate authority for itself, but it can acquire de facto control over outcomes that no one granted. The paper develops the principle of Decision Sovereignty, under which an institution, not the systems it deploys, owns its decisions and their execution. It introduces measurement constructs from the Decision Sovereignty Governance Methodology (DSGM): an eight-level A-scale; Permitted AI Authority (PAA) and Effective AI Authority (EAA), read on the same scale; the Authority Gap between them; and Choice Architecture Control (CAC), which captures a system's power over the options humans see. It traces a sequence of failure, from authority drift through judgment displacement and an accountability vacuum to legitimacy collapse, and sets out a governing discipline of six authority questions that together form an Authority Charter. The paper positions Authority Exposure as a risk category that complements the AI-First Risk Intelligence Framework (AIRIF™) and closes with testable propositions. This working paper presents the core argument of the author's forthcoming book, Capability Is Not Authority: Why Institutions Must Remain Sovereign Over the Systems They Deploy (AIRIF Press), and builds on AIRIF™: AI-First Risk Intelligence Framework (AIRIF Press, 2026; ISBN 979-8-9982544-0-6) and the author's earlier working paper (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24323708).

documents.abstract: This article examines civil liability for damages caused to individuals as a result of incorrect, outdated, or unreliable legal advice provided through artificial intelligence (AI). It explores the specific characteristics of damage arising from AI-based legal services, the identification of liable parties, the challenges of establishing damage and causation, and the legal status of service providers, developers, legal professionals, and users. The civil legislation of the Republic of Uzbekistan and regulatory frameworks governing artificial intelligence are comparatively analyzed in light of international experience. Based on the findings, the article proposes a differential liability model aimed at allocating liability according to the functional roles, obligations, fault, and causal contribution of each party to the occurrence of damage. The proposed model distinguishes between the mechanism for compensating the injured party and the internal recourse relationships among the parties involved.
