Purpose. To estimate regulation-specific pre-post changes after an eight-session peer-mentoring programme in Colombian youth swimmers and assess robustness to missing items, distributional assumptions and participant inclusion. Materials and methods. This single-group pilot study analysed all 29 swimmers aged 10–14 years with paired Sport Motivation Scale (SMS-28) records. Seven four-item regulations were scored on the original 1–7 metric when at least three items were available. Mean changes received bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs; 20,000 resamples), paired t tests and Cohen’s dz. Monte Carlo sign-flip tests (200,000 resamples), Wilcoxon tests, 20% trimmed-mean tests, Holm correction, reliability estimates and inclusion sensitivities assessed robustness. Results. Five of 1,624 item responses were missing (0.31%). Changes were small and imprecise: intrinsic motivation to know +0.27 (95% CI [−0.11, 0.75]; dz = 0.22), intrinsic motivation to accomplish +0.29 (95% CI [−0.27, 0.70]; dz = 0.22), intrinsic motivation to experience stimulation −0.01 (95% CI [−0.26, 0.21]; dz = −0.02), identified regulation −0.10 (95% CI [−0.54, 0.36]; dz = −0.08), introjected regulation +0.26 (95% CI [−0.39, 0.82]; dz = 0.15), external regulation +0.11 (95% CI [−0.47, 0.52]; dz = 0.08), and amotivation +0.28 (95% CI [−0.43, 0.90]; dz = 0.15). All Holm-adjusted primary p values were 1.00. Omitting two paired records changed intrinsic-accomplishment p from .24 (n = 29) to .02 (n = 27). The age-eligible sensitivity was unchanged. Conclusions. The programme coincided with no clear regulation-specific motivational shift. Complete inclusion and theory-consistent scoring reversed the former favourable conclusion, supporting controlled, fidelity-monitored evaluation rather than causal claims.

This study examines how national culture and gender shape job expectations in South America by comparing the importance Brazilian and Peruvian participants assign to 25 intrinsic and extrinsic job characteristics. While previous research has examined cultural or gender differences separately, this study evaluates whether gender differences vary across cultural contexts, clarifying the joint influence of culture and gender on work values. Data were collected from 916 Brazilian and Peruvian participants who rated job characteristics on a five-point scale. Mean rankings, MANCOVA/ANCOVA tests, and post hoc comparisons assessed cultural, gender, and interaction effects while controlling for age and employment status. Spearman rank-order correlations evaluated similarity in value hierarchies, and intrinsic–extrinsic composites examined broader motivational patterns. Results revealed significant main effects for both national culture and gender, with culture explaining the largest share of variance. Brazilian participants placed greater importance on intrinsic characteristics such as accomplishment, intellectual stimulation, and development, whereas Peruvian participants emphasized structure, routine, and stability. Female participants consistently rated both intrinsic and extrinsic characteristics as more important than males across most items and showed greater within-group homogeneity in their responses. Importantly, interaction effects indicated that gender differences did not manifest uniformly across countries, supporting the cultural contingency of gender role expectations. This study advances cross-cultural research on work values by jointly examining cultural, gender, and interaction effects within two economically interconnected South American countries. It contributes to Self-Determination Theory and Social Role Theory by demonstrating how motivational orientations vary across cultural environments and gendered socialization processes. The findings have practical implications for recruitment, job design, and talent management strategies, suggesting that organizations operating in South American contexts should tailor their approaches to reflect both cultural context and gender-specific motivational profiles when attracting and retaining talent.

As AI transitions to sociotechnical deployments, uninterpretable models pose serious threats to reliability, public trust and contestability. However, not all interpretation methods are created equal: for interpretability to enhance deployment safety and effectiveness, interpretation methods must be evaluated in a tiered system to differentiate evidence levels of trustworthiness, rather than validated through isolated interpretation instances. Our core vision is that elevating the evaluation of interpretation methods to a core AI assessment metric will drive robust knowledge discovery from data (KDD) and ensure safe, contestable sociotechnical deployments of AI. To this end, we propose TRUST, a tiered evaluation framework that builds upon the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) principles for Veridical Data Science (VDS) and the Predictive, Descriptive and Relevant (PDR) foundations. To differentiate interpretation methods effectively and systematically, TRUST grades interpretation across five tiers: Task-Aligned PDR Foundations, Rigorous Epistemic Grounding, Unifying Semantic Understanding, Scope Transferability, and Targeted Prospective Validation. We present a start-to-finish case study of the iterative Random Forest (iRF) family under TRUST and contrast it with other LLM interpretation methods that struggle to clear specific tiers. Finally, we conclude with brief initial thoughts on how TRUST principles can extend in autonomous agentic frameworks. Ultimately, the TRUST framework fosters contestability and epistemic grounding as foundational evaluation principles for human-machine workflows and, eventually, autonomous agentic workflows.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reduces the effort of learning tasks, but its effect on students’ higher-order thinking may depend on what is offloaded. This pre-registered systematic review synthesized 26 studies (2024–2026), identified from 4729 records, that measured cognitive load and higher-order thinking in the same higher education sample. Across 21 experimental studies, GenAI conditions most often showed lower load (12 studies) and better higher-order outcomes (14 studies). Lower load coincided with poorer thinking in three studies, none of high quality, and in all three the tool was positioned to perform the target thinking. Most outcomes were self-reports or products created using the available tool, and the only study assessing thinking after the tool was withdrawn found a decline. We propose, as a hypothesis, that offloading supports learning when the tool takes over preparatory work but may undermine it when the tool takes over the thinking the task should exercise.

Araştırma, puan sistemleri, şans çarkları, mini oyunlar ve sürpriz kutu mekanikleri gibi oyunlaştırma unsurlarının içsel motivasyon (algılanan keyif, merak) ve dışsal motivasyon (algılanan ekonomik fayda) üzerindeki etkilerini; bu motivasyonel süreçlerin oyunlaştırılmış özellikleri kullanma niyeti ve satın alma niyetiyle ilişkisini ve kaybetme korkusunun (FOMO) bu ilişkilerdeki moderatör rolünü yapısal eşitlik modellemesiyle test etmektedir. Veriler, Türkiye'deki mobil alışveriş uygulamalarında oyunlaştırma etkinliklerine katılmış 223 kullanıcıdan anket yöntemiyle toplanmış; ölçüm modeli doğrulayıcı faktör analizi, yapısal model ise bootstrap destekli SEM ile değerlendirilmiştir. Bulgular, oyunlaştırmanın hem merakı (β = .693) hem de algılanan keyfi (β = .559) anlamlı biçimde artırdığını; ancak içsel motivasyon unsurlarının satın alma niyeti üzerindeki etkisinin sınırlı kaldığını ortaya koymaktadır. Buna karşın, algılanan ekonomik faydanın satın alma niyeti üzerindeki etkisi modeldeki en güçlü ilişki olarak öne çıkmaktadır (β = .701). Kaybetme korkusunun ise öngörülen moderatör etkiyi sergilemediği; bunun yerine satın alma niyeti üzerinde bağımsız bir doğrudan etki oluşturduğu saptanmıştır (β = .144). Bu bulgular, oyunlaştırma tasarımında dışsal teşviklerin ve kıtlık temelli unsurların stratejik önemini desteklemektedir.

Background Digital mental health tools generate growing volumes of active and passive behavioral data, but integrating these data into clinical care and returning them to patients as usable feedback remains a major challenge. Artificial intelligence (AI), including large language models, are able to interpret such data and draft personalized feedback, offering a potentially scalable way to support this work. Whether AI can be adopted for this purpose, however, may depend less on its technical performance than on whether patients trust and accept it. This study examined how former and current patients in mental health service perceive AI involvement in delivering data-report feedback, comparing fully human (no AI), AI-assisted (hybrid), and fully AI-generated formats. Methods Twenty-five adults who had received outpatient mental health treatment viewed six standardized videos representing two clinical scenarios and the three delivery formats. Participants rated each video using a seven-item acceptability scale, compared the formats, and answered open-ended questions. They were not told which formats used AI until after completing the initial ratings. Results Acceptability differed across formats, F(1.20, 28.7) = 21.22, p < .001. Fully human feedback (mean 6.00) and AI-assisted feedback delivered by a human (mean 5.93) received similar ratings, and both were rated more favorably than fully AI-delivered feedback (mean 4.65). Participants were also more comfortable with AI analyzing their data when a human delivered the feedback than with AI both analyzing and delivering it. Overall, 23 of 25 participants preferred a format that retained human involvement after AI use was disclosed. Participants valued AI for producing clear and thorough summaries but wanted a person to explain and discuss the results. Conclusions Patients accepted AI-generated mental health feedback when a human remained involved in reviewing or delivering it. These findings support using AI to assist with data analysis and report preparation rather than replacing the human interaction involved in mental health care. Larger studies should test this approach in routine clinical settings.

documents.abstract: Background The World Health Organization classifies burnout as an occupational phenomenon, and artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how it arises. Research on AI and worker health has centered on what employees lose once displaced, not their behavior beforehand. We reasoned that the anticipation of being replaced would prompt a defensive form of overwork, and that this overwork may account for the association between anticipated replacement and burnout. Conservation of Resources theory explains why: facing threatened resources, employees invest still more to protect them, until the investment depletes what it should preserve. Methods We surveyed full-time employees in China’s information and communication technology (ICT) industry, where AI has reshaped job content and skills, across two waves, 1 month apart. Perceived AI job displacement, job meaningfulness, and workaholism (Dutch Work Addiction Scale) were measured at Time 1; burnout at Time 2 (emotional exhaustion subscale, Maslach Burnout Inventory–General Survey). Of 531 first-wave respondents, 337 completed both; attrition was related mainly to demographics, and inverse-probability-weighted estimates matched the results. Confirmatory factor analysis supported construct validity; we tested the moderated mediation with hierarchical regression and bootstrapped conditional process analysis (10,000 resamples). Results Perceived AI job displacement was positively associated with burnout (β = 0.54, p < 0.001) and workaholism (β = 0.41, p < 0.001), with a significant indirect path via workaholism (0.09, 95% CI [0.04, 0.13]). Job meaningfulness did not buffer this association; it amplified it (interaction β = 0.14, p < 0.01). The displacement–workaholism association was about twice as strong at high job meaningfulness (b = 0.44, p < 0.001) as at low (b = 0.21, p < 0.01), and the conditional indirect effect on burnout rose from 0.06 (95% CI [0.02, 0.10]) to 0.12 (95% CI [0.06, 0.19]). The index of moderated mediation was significant (0.05, 95% CI [0.01, 0.10]). Conclusion Among these ICT employees, perceived AI job displacement was associated with higher burnout a month later, and workaholism may account for it. The indirect association was strongest where least expected: among employees who found their work most meaningful. Intensified effort warrants scrutiny rather than approval, and workplace health surveillance during digital transformation may consider treating a sudden escalation of overwork as a potential early warning of burnout.

The present study examined the relationship between perceived teacher support and student engagement at the undergraduate level. Perceived teacher support was conceptualized through four dimensions: emotional support, academic support, autonomy support, and classroom structure, while student engagement comprised behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory, the study emphasized the role of supportive learning environments in enhancing student motivation and engagement. A quantitative correlational research design was employed. The sample consisted of 300 undergraduate students selected from four universities, including two public and two private universities. Equal representation was ensured across institution type, with 150 students from public and 150 from private universities. Each university contributed 75 students, including 38 males and 37 females. Perceived teacher support was measured by adapting validated open-access instruments, including the Perceived Teacher Support Scale (PTSS), the Foreign Language Teacher Support Scale (FLTSS), and the Questionnaire on Teacher Support Adaptivity (QTSA). Student engagement was measured using the Student Engagement Instrument (SEI). Data were analyzed to examine levels of perceived teacher support and student engagement, differences based on gender and institution type, and the relationship between the two variables. The findings revealed a significant positive relationship between perceived teacher support and student engagement, indicating that supportive teaching practices enhance behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement among undergraduate students. The study highlights the importance of teacher support in fostering meaningful engagement and offers practical implications for improving teaching practices and learning environments in higher education.
